topicName: Debugging and Troubleshooting Failing Pods and Nodes
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Debugging and Troubleshooting Failing Pods and Nodes in Kubernetes"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Kubernetes environments can occasionally experience unexpected failures at the Pod or Node level. This tutorial provides a structured, step-by-step approach to diagnosing and resolving these issues efficiently using standard kubectl commands."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. Troubleshooting Failing Pods"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"When a Pod fails, it typically enters a non-running state such as CrashLoopBackOff, ImagePullBackOff, or Pending. Follow these steps to isolate the root cause."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Check the Pod status and restart counts using 'kubectl get pods'."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Inspect the Pod events and configuration details using 'kubectl describe pod <pod-name>'."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Review application logs using 'kubectl logs <pod-name> --previous' if the container crashed."},{"order":8,"type":"code","text":"kubectl get pods --all-namespaces
kubectl describe pod web-app-deployment-5d758f-abc12"},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Common Pod Failure Modes"},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"CrashLoopBackOff: The application inside the container is exiting with a non-zero code. Check logs for uncaught exceptions or missing environment variables."},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"ImagePullBackOff: Kubernetes cannot download the container image. Verify image tags, container registry credentials, and network connectivity."},{"order":12,"type":"bullet_point","text":"OOMKilled: Out Of Memory. The container exceeded its memory limit. Increase the memory limit in the Pod specification or optimize the application."},{"order":13,"type":"subheading","text":"3. Troubleshooting Failing Nodes"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"If multiple Pods fail across a specific worker node, the underlying node itself may be experiencing resource exhaustion, networking partitions, or kubelet failures."},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Check overall cluster node health using 'kubectl get nodes'."},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Inspect node conditions such as MemoryPressure, DiskPressure, and Ready status using 'kubectl describe node <node-name>'."},{"order":17,"type":"code","text":"kubectl get nodes -o wide
kubectl describe node worker-node-1"},{"order":18,"type":"subheading","text":"4. Remediation and Recovery"},{"order":19,"type":"paragraph","text":"Once the failing component is identified, apply the appropriate remediation steps to restore cluster stability."},{"order":20,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Drain a malfunctioning node safely before performing maintenance using 'kubectl drain <node-name> --ignore-daemonsets'."},{"order":21,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Delete stuck terminating pods forcefully if necessary using 'kubectl delete pod <pod-name> --grace-period=0 --force'."},{"order":22,"type":"code","text":"kubectl drain worker-node-1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
kubectl uncordon worker-node-1"}]
